summary: The land receives a seventh-year Sabbath, and the fiftieth-year Jubilee proclaims liberty, returns Israelite families to ancestral property, and limits prices by the harvest years remaining. The chapter then regulates land and house redemption, interest-free support, Israelite debt service and release, while also explicitly permitting permanent, inheritable enslavement of foreigners.
whyItMatters: Leviticus 25 restrains permanent land loss and harsh debt service among Israelites, but its unequal protection of Israelite kin and foreign slaves prevents Jubilee from being presented as universal emancipation.

context.author: Leviticus presents Yahweh speaking these land and labor rules to Moses at Sinai; the finished book does not name its narrator, and its composition history remains debated.
context.audience: Israelite landholders, buyers, lenders, poor kin, servants, resident foreigners, and families involved in redemption or release.
context.date: The laws are narrated at Mount Sinai and anticipate settled life in Canaan; the date of the book's received literary form is debated.
context.setting: Future Israelite agriculture, towns, households, property transfers, debt, and labor in the land described as Yahweh's.
context.literaryForm: Land-tenure and household economic law structured by Sabbath-year and Jubilee cycles, redemption cases, and exodus-based limits.

outline.heading: The land's seventh-year Sabbath
outline.note: Sowing, pruning, and formal harvesting cease while the land's produce feeds the whole household, foreigners, livestock, and wildlife.

outline.heading: Jubilee liberty, return, and fair pricing
outline.note: The fiftieth year returns people to family property and makes sale value depend on harvest years remaining.

outline.heading: Provision during rest and Yahweh's ownership
outline.note: A promised sixth-year yield answers the food question, and permanent land sale is barred because the land belongs to Yahweh.

outline.heading: Fields, houses, and Levitical property
outline.note: Kinsmen and sellers may redeem land, while walled-city houses and Levitical holdings receive distinct rules.

outline.heading: Supporting an impoverished Israelite
outline.note: The community must uphold poor kin and may not profit through interest on money or food.

outline.heading: Israelite debt service and foreign slavery
outline.note: Israelite kin are treated as hired residents and released, while foreigners may be purchased, owned, and inherited permanently.

outline.heading: An Israelite serving a resident foreigner
outline.note: Kin redemption, year-based pricing, protection from harsh rule, and Jubilee release apply because Israelites belong as servants to Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
keyVerses.why: Jubilee proclaims liberty and return to family and property.

keyVerses.text: “‘The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine; for you are strangers and live as foreigners with me.
keyVerses.why: God’s ownership is the stated reason land cannot be permanently sold.

keyVerses.text: You may make them an inheritance for your children after you, to hold for a possession. Of them you may take your slaves forever, but over your brothers the children of Israel you shall not rule, one over another, with harshness.
keyVerses.why: Foreign slaves may be inherited and held permanently, limiting the scope of the chapter’s release rules.

questions.question: What is the Sabbath year for the land?
questions.answer: After six years of sowing, pruning, and gathering, the seventh is a solemn rest with no planned sowing or pruning and no formal harvest of volunteer growth. What the land produces remains food for household members, workers, resident foreigners, livestock, and wild animals.

questions.question: What does Jubilee mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: After seven cycles of seven years, the fiftieth year is declared holy with a trumpet on the Day of Atonement. It brings rest from cultivation and returns Israelites to family and ancestral property; the chapter prescribes this system but does not narrate a historical observance of it.

questions.question: How does Jubilee affect a land sale price?
questions.answer: Buyer and seller are told to price the number of crops remaining before the next Jubilee, increasing the price when many years remain and decreasing it when few remain. The transaction is therefore temporary use of harvests, not unlimited ownership of the land.

questions.question: What does “the land is mine” change?
questions.answer: It prevents Israelite land from being sold permanently and describes the inhabitants themselves as strangers and resident foreigners with Yahweh. That claim underlies the right of redemption and the eventual return of rural property.

questions.question: Are all houses released in the Jubilee?
questions.answer: No. A house in a walled city becomes permanent after a one-year redemption window, while village houses follow field rules and are released. Houses in Levitical cities remain redeemable and return in Jubilee, and their pasture fields may not be sold.

questions.question: How must the community respond before poor kin sell themselves?
questions.answer: The community must support an impoverished Israelite so that he can continue living among them, described as living like an alien or temporary resident. They may not charge interest on money lent to him or profit on food supplied to him. The following reminder of liberation from Egypt grounds this duty.

questions.question: What limits apply when an Israelite sells himself to another Israelite?
questions.answer: He is not to be made to serve as a slave but treated as a hired or temporary resident until Jubilee, when he and his children return to family and property. Harsh rule and permanent sale are forbidden because Yahweh brought Israelites out of Egyptian slavery.

questions.question: Does Jubilee free the foreign slaves named in verses 44-46?
questions.answer: No. The text permits buying people from surrounding nations and resident-alien families, calls them property, and allows them to be inherited by the owner’s children and held permanently. The promised release for Israelite debt servants does not extend to these foreign slaves.

questions.question: What happens if an impoverished Israelite is sold to a wealthy resident foreigner?
questions.answer: The Israelite retains a right of redemption by self or close kin at a price based on years remaining to Jubilee. He must be treated as a year-by-year hired servant without harsh rule and, if not redeemed earlier, leaves with his children in the Jubilee.

glossary.def: The fiftieth year of land rest, liberty, family return, and restoration of Israelite ancestral property.
Buying back land, a house, or an Israelite debt servant under the chapter's kinship and year-based rules.
Profit charged on money or food, which the chapter forbids when supporting impoverished Israelite kin.
A person held in service or ownership; the chapter sharply distinguishes temporary Israelite debt service from permanent foreign slavery.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding chapter has regulated sanctuary service and judged a camp offense, closing with equal law for foreigner and native-born in that legal unit. The focus now shifts to land, property, poverty, and service.

here.text: Land rest and Jubilee limit Israelite loss of family property and debt service. Distinct rules govern houses and Levitical holdings, while foreign slaves may be bought and inherited permanently.

after.text: Chapter 26 links obedience to harvest, security, and God’s presence, then threatens famine and exile for persistent refusal. It explicitly says the desolate land will receive the Sabbaths it had been denied.
